title: Electromagnetism: Fields, Forces and Induction
standard_text: Electric fields and forces on charges; magnetic fields; forces on current-carrying conductors and moving charges; magnetic flux, Faraday's and Lenz's laws; DC motors, AC generators, transformers and power transmission. (Senior Secondary Physics, Unit 3: Gravity and electromagnetism)
meta_desc: Free Year 12 Physics worksheets on electromagnetism: electric fields, F = BIL, F = qvB, magnetic flux, Faraday's and Lenz's laws, motors, generators and transformers. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: F = BIL sin θ; F = qvB sin θ.
body_html:
How to think about it

An electric field exerts a force F = qE on a charge; between parallel plates E = V/d. A magnetic field exerts a force on a current (F = BIL) and on a moving charge (F = qvB), at right angles to the motion: this drives electric motors and bends charged particles into circles.

A changing magnetic flux induces an e.m.f. (Faraday's law), in a direction that opposes the change (Lenz's law). Generators and transformers use induction; high-voltage transmission reduces I²R losses.

Example

Wire 0.20 m, 3.0 A, at 90° to 0.50 T. Force?

F = BIL = 0.50 × 3.0 × 0.20

Answer: 0.30 N

Example

Transformer: 240 V, 1000 primary turns, 50 secondary turns. Vs?

Vs = 240 × 50 ÷ 1000

Answer: 12 V

Common mistakes

  • Using the left hand instead of the right hand for the rule.
  • Thinking a steady magnetic field induces a current.
  • Thinking a transformer works with DC.

faq.q: Why is power transmitted at high voltage?
faq.a: P = VI, so a higher voltage means a smaller current for the same power, and the heat lost in the lines (I²R) is much smaller.

faq.q: What does Lenz's law tell us?
faq.a: The induced current always opposes the change in flux that caused it, which is why you must do work to push a magnet into a coil.
